new_statements.quote: Twenty six segmental phonemes and nine suprasegmental phonemes are identified. They are five vowel phonemes, twenty consonant phonemes, one phoneme of length, two junctures, four pitch levels and three terminals. [p. 102] ... The following suprasegmental features have been found to be phonemic: Junctures: 1. / - / Open juncture 2. / + / Close juncture. Pitch levels: 1. / 1 / Low 2. / 2 / Mid 3. / 3 / High 4. / 4 / Extra high. Terminals 1. Rising 2. Falling 3. Level [p. 172; terminal symbols omitted, scanned-garbled] ... In these combinations a difference is observed between the constituents in terms of prominence. ... Emphatic constituent has the highest pitch level. [p. 179]
new_statements.citation: Rajendran, Nanu. 1978. Description of the Language of Muḍugas. PhD thesis, University of Kerala, Trivandrum. Chapter 1 'Phonemics'.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 1 Phonemics: §1.0 Inventory of Phonemes, p. 102 (PDF p. 2); §1.5 Suprasegmental phonemes, p. 172 (PDF p. 73); §1.5.5.1.1 Phrase intonation, p. 179 (PDF p. 80)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only primary phonological description posits no stress phoneme at all: the phonemic suprasegmentals are vowel/consonant length, two junctures (open/close), four pitch levels and three terminal contours. Prominence within phrases is treated as pitch level (e.g. numeral/adjective + noun: higher pitch on the noun; coordinate members equal; elsewhere the first word higher; emphatic constituent highest). No statement locates a stressed syllable within the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source never mentions stress or accent (0 hits for stress/accent and scanned variants in the 216-page chapter).
new_statements.domain_note: Negative by exhaustive enumeration of suprasegmental phonemes, not an explicit sentence 'Muduga has no word stress'. Pitch levels are illustrated on words and sentences; §1.5.5 covers 2- and 3-word phrases in isolation. Data: Muduga of Attappady, 1970s fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Muduga (Mudugar) of the Attappady valley, Palakkad, Kerala = mudu1239 (Rajendran's 1970s fieldwork; Kapp's informants from Pettikkallu). Not to be confused with Muduva/Muthuvan of Idukki (muth1236), which the Encyclopaedia (1996: 274) warns the Census conflates with Muduga; also distinct from Mudu Koraga (mudu1241) and Vitu/Muduapa (mudu1242).

sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonemics (pp. 101-316) posits 26 segmental and 9 suprasegmental phonemes: length, two junctures, four pitch levels, three terminals (§1.0 p. 102; §1.5 p. 172). Stress is not among the suprasegmentals and the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the 216-page chapter (grep incl. scanned-garbled variants). Word prominence in phrases is described as pitch level (§1.5.5, pp. 179-181: 'Emphatic constituent has the highest pitch level'; numeral/adjective + noun -> higher pitch on the noun; elsewhere first word higher).

sources.citation: Ravindran, P.N., C.G. Syama & S.K. Syam [Shyam] (with K.S. Pradeep Kumar & Mini P.V.). 2017. Descriptive Grammar of Muduga and Kurumba Languages. Calicut: KIRTADS. 318 pp.
sources.note: Part I Muduga, Ch. II 'Phoneme identification' (pp. 38-51): 5 vowels, 21 consonants, clusters, gemination, distribution. Nothing on stress, accent or suprasegmentals (the only 'stress' hit is a generic definition of morphology on p. 151, Kurumba part).

sources.citation: Madhava Menon, T. (ed.). 1996. The Encyclopaedia of Dravidian Tribes, Vol. II. Thiruvananthapuram: International School of Dravidian Linguistics. Entries 'MUDUGA' (pp. 267-273) and 'MUDUGA LANGUAGE' (pp. 274-276).
sources.note: 'Phonology' paragraph (p. 274) summarises Rajendran: vowel system like Malayalam, fewer consonant phonemes, no palatal/velar/dental nasals, voiced stops present, sound correspondences. Silent on stress.
